vignette:
Margaret's Vigil

Margaret sits in the waiting room with her hands folded in her lap, her posture still carrying the rigid discipline of thirty-seven years on the force. At seventy-one, she's been retired for four years, but her shoulders remain squared, her jaw set in the particular way of someone trained to manage crisis. Today, she's here because her husband finally insisted. "You're not sleeping," he'd said last week. "You're not living."

It was eighteen months ago when the call came through—the kind every parent dreads, the kind Margaret had delivered to countless other families during her career. Her son, Daniel, thirty-eight years old, had been struck by a car while cycling to work. The driver had run a red light. Daniel was in intensive care for six days before the injuries proved incompatible with life.

Margaret describes the hospital waiting room with photographic precision: the exact shade of the linoleum, the broken vending machine, the way the fluorescent lights hummed. She can recite the names of every nurse who cared for Daniel, the exact words the doctor used when he said there was nothing more they could do. Her training as a police officer—decades spent documenting crime scenes, interviewing witnesses, maintaining emotional distance to do the job—became a curse in those days. Her mind recorded everything with crystalline clarity, as if Daniel's death were evidence to be catalogued.

Since then, Margaret has been unable to sleep through the night. She wakes at 2:47 a.m., always the same time, her heart racing, sometimes unsure whether she's in the hospital or at home. She lies beside her sleeping husband, Tom, and feels a peculiar isolation—as if there's a pane of glass between her and the rest of the world. Tom tries to reach her, but she finds his touch sometimes unbearable, though she can't quite explain why. Other times, she grips his hand so tightly he winces.

The worst moments come without warning. Last month, a young man on a bicycle passed their house, and Margaret found herself unable to breathe, her hands shaking so violently she couldn't hold her coffee cup. A car horn made her flinch so sharply she nearly fell. She's stopped going to the grocery store because the crowds feel suffocating, because she's convinced something terrible will happen if she's not home, as if her vigilance alone prevents further loss.

Margaret has thrown herself into researching the accident—reading the police report repeatedly, studying traffic patterns at that intersection, reviewing the driver's record. Part of her still thinks like a detective, searching for some detail that might reframe what happened, make it make sense. She's attended every court hearing, sitting in the gallery with her hands clasped, watching the driver—a woman only five years older than herself—and feeling something between rage and a hollow emptiness.

What troubles her most is the guilt that surfaces unbidden. During her career, she'd missed Daniel's school plays, his soccer games, his graduation. She'd been present for the important moments, but distracted by work, by the weight of other people's traumas. Now she has all the time in the world, and her son is gone. She wonders if her absence somehow made him more vulnerable, less protected. She knows this isn't rational—the part of her that remains a trained investigator recognizes this as illogical—but knowing and feeling are different things.

Tom keeps saying she needs to "move forward," but Margaret doesn't know what that means. Moving forward feels like betrayal, like accepting that her son's absence is simply something to accommodate rather than something that has fundamentally broken the world.
